sections.text: Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) is not more accurate than BMI at everything, but it answers a question BMI cannot: where is the weight carried? WHtR is waist circumference divided by height, both in the same unit, and the simple target is a ratio under 0.5, meaning a waist less than half your height. BMI only compares weight with height. The two measures work best together, and NICE guidance recommends WHtR for assessing central fat, especially in adults with a BMI below 35.

NICE's obesity guidance (NG246), as summarised in a published review, describes WHtR of 0.4 to 0.49 as healthy central adiposity with no increased health risks, 0.5 to 0.59 as increased central adiposity with elevated risks, and 0.6 or more as high central adiposity with further increased risks. The simple message to patients is to keep the waist to half of height. The same summary says WHtR is recommended for adults, especially those with a BMI under 35, and particularly for people from South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean backgrounds, or those with high muscle mass.

Our healthy weight and overweight calculators use a very similar scheme: under 0.4 flagged as possibly underweight, under 0.5 healthy, 0.5 up to 0.6 increased risk, and 0.6 and above high risk. The CDC, for its part, describes BMI as a screening measure that does not show how fat is distributed, which is the gap WHtR fills.
Because the target depends on height, the waist that counts as healthy changes with it. The table converts the 0.5 and 0.6 lines into waist sizes, with inches rounded to one decimal.

This is why a fixed waist number is a poor guide. The same 90 cm waist gives a ratio of 0.563 at 160 cm tall, 0.529 at 170 cm and 0.500 at 180 cm. In inches, a 35 in waist is 0.486 for someone 72 in (6 ft) tall but 0.547 for someone 64 in (5 ft 4 in) tall.
Worked example: where BMI and WHtR disagree

Assumptions: four hypothetical adults. BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, categorised with the CDC adult cutoffs (18.5, 25 and 30). WHtR is waist divided by height, in centimetres, read against the NICE bands above.

Person 1 is the BMI false alarm: the number says overweight while the waist is well under half of height (half of 185 cm is 92.5 cm). Person 2 is the opposite: BMI looks fine, but half of 170 cm is 85 cm and the waist is 90 cm, so WHtR flags a larger waist than the weight suggests. Persons 3 and 4 are cases where both agree. Neither measure replaces a clinical assessment, but the disagreements are the reason to take both.
What WHtR can and cannot do

The same published review reports that multiple meta-analyses found WHtR predicted type 2 diabetes with higher accuracy than BMI in several populations, and that BMI cannot tell lean mass from fat mass. WHtR adds information about central fat. But it has limits of its own. A tape measure introduces error, and a waist measurement says nothing about muscle, bone or the organs. A single reading, taken once, is not a diagnosis of anything, and the bands describe risk in groups of people, not what will happen to you.
How to measure the waist consistently

Our calculators ask for the waist at navel level, and the healthy weight calculator mentions the narrowest point for women. Different guidelines use different landmarks, so the key is to choose one and use it every time. Stand relaxed, breathe out normally, keep the tape level and snug without squeezing the skin, and do not pull your stomach in. Time of day, a recent meal and posture can all shift the number, so measure under similar conditions, take two or three readings and average them.

items: Comparing your waist with an absolute number from a chart instead of with your own height.
Mixing units, for example waist in inches over height in centimetres.
Measuring over clothing, or at a different spot each time.
Treating a result of 0.49 as safe and 0.51 as unsafe. The bands are broad guides, and a change of a few millimetres moves the ratio across a line.
Using WHtR on its own. Use it with BMI, and with body fat or blood pressure and blood tests if your doctor suggests them.

sections.text: BMI and waist-to-height ratio are screening tools, not diagnoses. A ratio above 0.5 is a prompt to look at lifestyle and talk to a clinician, who can consider blood pressure, blood tests and your wider health. This is especially true if your waist has grown without explanation.
